Caching 101

Making a slow API feel fast

Dana Levi · Backend Guild, May 2026

Welcome. Twenty minutes, questions at the end. Ask how many people have shipped a cache bug to production: usually most of the room.

When is a cache worth it?

  • The same question is asked again and again
  • The answer changes rarely
  • Computing it is slow or costs money
  • A slightly old answer is acceptable
Reveal the four conditions one by one. Stress the last one: if stale data is never acceptable, a cache is the wrong tool and the query itself has to get faster.

Where a cache can live

BrowserHTTP headers, per user
CDNShared, close to the user
ApplicationMemory or Redis
DatabaseMaterialised views

Press the down arrow for the application tier in detail

In-process or shared?

In-process Shared (Redis)
Lookup time under 1 µs about 1 ms
Survives a deploy No Yes
Same answer on every server No Yes
Extra moving parts None One more service

Cache-aside in a dozen lines

async function getProfile(userId) {
  const key = `profile:${userId}`;

  const cached = await redis.get(key);
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached);

  const profile = await db.loadProfile(userId);
  await redis.set(key, JSON.stringify(profile), { EX: 300 });
  return profile;
}

async function updateProfile(userId, changes) {
  await db.saveProfile(userId, changes);
  await redis.del(`profile:${userId}`);
}

The hard part

“There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.”

Phil Karlton

Choosing a TTL

Data TTL Why
Country list 24 hours Changes a few times a year
User profile 5 minutes Deleted on every write anyway
Search results 30 seconds Fresh enough, absorbs bursts
Account balance Do not cache A stale answer is a wrong answer
The TTL is a business decision, not a technical one. Ask the product owner how old the answer may be, then pick the longest value they accept.

Takeaways

  1. Measure first, cache second
  2. Start with the tier closest to the user
  3. Decide how stale is acceptable before writing code
  4. Delete on write, expire on a timer
